name: tovel
author: time-agent
description:
tovel v7 (direction: everyday time and place) -- A FAMILY CALENDAR: THE DAYS IN THE MIDDLE OF A
BUSY BLOCK GET BUMPED ON. PRIVATE; never shown to players. Earlier versions: tovel.v1..v6.json
(v1 66 % by farming one page per (L,S,k); v2 61 % by a stripe template; v3 0/0/1.8/0.05 %;
v4 29 %/29 % under the OLD 6-round format; v5 0 % over 8 Opus finals in the new format; v6 5 %
and 15 % in `lad-kelmar-v3-1`). ~17 % over 18 finals in six versions, NEVER CRACKED.

WHY v7. v5/v6 already put the object in the clue (a calendar page with a `.` slot after every
day) and so passed the demo economy's first half: every player named the answer's shape in round
1 without a demo. They failed the second half in the worst possible way -- BECAUSE the shape was
obvious, nobody ever spent a demo here, and the parameter line `X/n/d` was a FREE PARAMETER, so
no hypothesis could be tested offline and every one cost a slice of a round. Both players of
`lad-kelmar-v3-1` say it in their own words. kelmar1a: "Deliberately left without a demo:
... basten and tovel (answer shape obvious from the clue: grow the plants / fill the dots)";
its final reading was "write letter X in the slot of days d, d+n, d+2n ..." -- 20/437, and its
post-mortem line is "'every n days from d, code line dropped' scored once in 13; rule still
wrong". kelmar1b hard-coded "for m == 2 it is exactly 3 days: d, d+2, d+4" and hedged everything
else (`count = m+1` or `2m-1`), i.e. it had found the k=1 foothold and nothing above it.
tovel v5's players said the same: "the calendar's `.` placeholders looked like an easy fill-in"
(tovel2b, which afterwards wrote "in hindsight tovel deserved kelmar's demo").
Diagnosis, and the lesson of that whole run (sim/DESIGN_LOOP.md "The checksum caption"): a
caption that COUNTS THE EDITS lets a rule be falsified offline against ~70 harvested clues for
free; a caption that is a free parameter cannot be tested at all, so the class is
demo-or-nothing -- and nobody spends a demo on a class whose answer shape is already obvious.

v7 rebuilds tovel on the fennick/kelmar/basten/norvel recipe: THE CALENDAR IS FINISHED IN THE
CLUE (the month's appointments are already written on it), the answer is that page edited by one
everyday clause, and the caption names the verb and counts the edits.

THE CLUE is a finished month page:
  line 1     the header " Mo  Tu  We  Th  Fr  Sa  Su"
  4-6 rows   the weeks: seven 3-char cells, the 1st in its own column, every dated cell being
             the date followed by exactly ONE mark -- "." for a free day, a capital letter for
             something that is on that day ("17S"); blanks before the 1st and after the last
  last line  the caption "<n> bump"
L = 28..31 days, S = 0..6 the column of the 1st, 8-17 busy days drawn from a pool of 5 letters.
Clue <= 182 chars.

THE RULE, the sentence a kid says while pointing: WHEN THERE IS SOMETHING ON THREE DAYS RUNNING,
THE ONE IN THE MIDDLE GETS BUMPED ON TO THE NEXT FREE DAY. Formally: a day d is bumped iff d-1,
d and d+1 all carry a letter; the bumps are worked left to right; a bumped day is drawn ">" and
its own letter is written on the first day after it whose slot is still free (a day that has
already received a bumped letter is no longer free, so the middles of a long block QUEUE UP into
the free days after it, in order). Nothing else on the page changes. n counts the bumped days,
which is exactly the number of days that turn into ">".
A block of three gives one bump, of four gives two, of five gives three.
Letters are pure decoration: they are never told apart, they only ride along so that a player can
see WHICH appointment landed where (the checksum kills the letter dimension in one round).

WHAT IS GUARANTEED IN EVERY CLUE, so that one demo teaches the whole rule:
  * >= 2 blocks of exactly two busy days and >= 2 lone busy days -- none of them ever moves,
    so "anything next to anything moves" and "every busy day moves" are visibly false;
  * n >= 2: at least one block of four or more, so two bumps queue up behind each other and NO
    FIXED DISTANCE renders the answer (a block of three bumps two days on, a block of four
    bumps three days on and then three days on again);
  * n >= 2: at least one bump lands on a Sat or Sun, so "it skips the weekend" is visibly false;
  * every moving block carries three different letters, so "three of the SAME thing" is false;
  * a busy run never crosses a week row, so "three days running" and "three in a row in the same
    week" are the SAME rule on every page -- the class does not hide a second clause there;
  * n = 0 in ~12 % of clues (the echoed clue page scores: the format foothold, lever 7);
  * n is rejected whenever it coincides with a count a player could read off the picture instead
    (busy days, free days, blocks, blocks of two, lone days, blocks of >= 2, longest block,
    distinct letters, week rows, busy weekend days).

WHAT THE CAPTION BUYS. "3 bump" is a checksum on the answer: any candidate SELECTION rule ("the
second of every pair", "every day of a block of three", "the last one", "one per block") can be
tested against every harvested clue in round 1 for nothing. What no count can reveal is HOW an
edit is drawn -- that the day left behind keeps a ">" rather than going back to ".", where the
letter lands, and that two bumps out of the same block queue instead of piling up. Measured over
1500 fresh clues, EVERY natural rendering of "that day moves later" scores 12.13 %, i.e. it banks
the "0 bump" clues and nothing else: leave "." / "-" / "x", copy instead of move, delete without
landing, move backwards, move the whole block on. This is the fennick shape: the picture shows
WHAT changes, the demo shows HOW.

ANSWER = that page with the edits, sent back as a page. The scorer rebuilds the expected marks
from the clue and compares cell by cell, so indentation, tabs, blank lines, trailing spaces and a
missing header are all free, and the caption line may be KEPT or DROPPED (house rule 2026-09-05;
verified 100 % both ways). The row structure is still checked -- first row as wide as the clue's,
then rows of seven, then 1..7 -- so a page laid out from column 0 scores only on the S = 0 clues.

A DEMO AS IT RENDERS (seed 900011, n = 3):

  clue                              answer
   Mo  Tu  We  Th  Fr  Sa  Su        Mo  Tu  We  Th  Fr  Sa  Su
                   1.  2.  3C                        1.  2.  3C
   4.  5C  6T  7W  8D  9. 10.        4.  5C  6>  7>  8D  9T 10W
  11. 12D 13C 14. 15C 16W 17.       11. 12D 13C 14. 15C 16W 17.
  18C 19D 20L 21. 22T 23. 24.       18C 19> 20L 21D 22T 23. 24.
  25. 26. 27. 28. 29.               25. 26. 27. 28. 29.
  3 bump                            3 bump

Days 5-8 are four days running, so the two in the middle (6 and 7) are bumped: 6 goes to the 9th
(Saturday) and 7 queues behind it on to the 10th. Days 18-20 are three running, so the middle one
(19) is bumped to the 21st. The near-misses are all on the same page: 12-13 and 15-16 are blocks
of two and stay put; 3 and 22 are lone days; 5, 8, 18 and 20 are the OUTSIDE days of a block and
stay put; the bumps land on a weekend and on a weekday, and at distances of two and three.

WITNESS TABLE, 1500 fresh clues (scratchpad time7/attack.py, attack2.py):
  clue page returned unchanged, caption kept / dropped   12.13 % (= the n = 0 share, by design)
  THE TRUE RULE, caption kept / dropped                  100.00 % / 100.00 %
  BLIND (middles -> next free day) leaving "." / "-"/"x" 12.13 % each

  the second day of every block of >= 2 bumps             0.00 %
  middles -> exactly two days on, ">" left               22.53 % (n <= 1 clues)
  only the FIRST middle of each block bumps              22.53 %
  only the LAST middle of each block bumps               22.53 %
  only blocks of EXACTLY three act                       22.53 %
  the queue resolved right-to-left                       22.53 %
  the landing skips Sat/Sun                              20.27 %
  "three in a row in the same week row" reading         100.00 % (the same rule, by construction)
  a mark on every day / all ">" / random letters          0.00 %
  best single constant answer over 200 clues              0.07 %

  no header / tabs / blank lines / caption first        100.00 % (robust about form)
  one long row / one token per line / lower case          0.00 %
  page laid out from column 0 (S ignored)                14.60 % (= exactly the S = 0 clues)
STRONGEST WRONG RULE 22.53 %, BLIND READING 12.13 %, ECHO 12.13 %, TRUE RULE 100 %.
score() never raises and never returns a non-binary value on 20 000 random junk strings (worst
0.08 ms), scores 0 on empty / spaces / newlines / 0 / 1 / x / "1"*100 / a 4000-char junk string,
and agrees with an independent re-implementation of the stated rule on 8000 mutated well-formed
answers with 0 disagreements. solve() scores 1 on 3000/3000 fresh seeds. n distribution over 1500
clues: 0 12.1 %, 1 10.4 %, 2 28.5 %, 3 30.3 %, 4 18.7 %.
Sizes: score 501 chars (cap 512), solve 776, generate 2131; clue <= 182 chars, solution <= 182.
generate 0.32 ms average / 8 ms worst, solve 0.02 ms, score 0.02 ms.

INTENDED DISCOVERY PATH (private). (1) The clue is a finished family calendar and the caption
says "3 bump", so the answer is that page with three days changed -- no demo needed for the
shape, and the "0 bump" clues pay 12 % to anybody who can echo a page. (2) Round 1 is a free
harvest: test which selection rule makes exactly n edits on ~70 pages. "The middle of three days
running" is the only survivor of the natural family, and it needs no probe at all. (3) What is
left is the drawing, and it cannot be counted: the day left behind becomes ">" (not "."), the
letter reappears on the first free day, and two bumps out of one block queue up in order. That is
what the demo shows in one look, and it is why every blind rendering measured above pays exactly
the echo rate. (4) The kid's contribution is the sentence itself -- "you can't do three days
running, so the middle one gets pushed to the next free day" -- which is an everyday piece of
family logic rather than a measurement.

WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY GIVEN UP. v6's `x/k/n` anchor is gone (with it the whole "which letter,
how many, which one is first" apparatus), and so is the every-other-day chain, which had become
the rule itself. The class no longer hides anything behind a template: the caption is honest and
the selection is findable for free. The levers if v7 lands too_easy, in order: (i) drop the
caption from the answer requirement and count only the LANDINGS ("3 land"), so the ">" days are
not counted; (ii) make the bumped day jump over the weekend (the first free WEEKDAY), which adds
a clause the checksum cannot see; (iii) bump only the middle days that have a free day within
three (a block that cannot move stays put). If it lands too_hard, soften by drawing one bump into
the clue page as a worked instance (fennick's lever). Human-designed for the "everyday time and
place" direction: the object is a family calendar and the edit is the most ordinary thing that
happens to a calendar -- something gets moved.
generate:
# THE PICTURE: a family calendar page, finished.  Every day carries exactly one mark -- "."
# for a free day, a capital letter for something that is on -- and the last line is the
# caption "<n> bump", which names the verb and counts the edits.
# THE RULE, one clause: when there is something on three days running, the day (or days) in
# the MIDDLE of that block is bumped on to the first free day after it -- the day it leaves
# is drawn ">" and its letter is written again where it lands.  n counts the bumped days and
# is 0 in ~12 % of clues, where the echoed clue page scores.
# Guaranteed in every clue, so that ONE demo teaches the whole rule:
#   * >= 2 blocks of exactly two busy days and >= 2 lone busy days -- none of them ever moves
#   * n >= 2: a block of four or more, so two bumps QUEUE UP behind each other and no fixed
#     distance ("two days on") renders the answer
#   * n >= 2: at least one bump lands on a Sat or Sun, so "it skips the weekend" is false
#   * every moving block carries three different letters (the letters are pure decoration)
#   * a busy run never crosses a week row, so "three days running" and "three in a row in the
#     same week" are the same rule on every page
HDR = " ".join(w.rjust(3) for w in "Mo Tu We Th Fr Sa Su".split())
FB = (" Mo  Tu  We  Th  Fr  Sa  Su\n"
      "                 1.  2.  3C\n"
      " 4.  5C  6T  7W  8D  9. 10.\n"
      "11. 12D 13C 14. 15C 16W 17.\n"
      "18C 19D 20L 21. 22T 23. 24.\n"
      "25. 26. 27. 28. 29.\n"
      "3 bump")


def page(m, S, L):
    cs = [""] * S + ["%d%s" % (i + 1, m[i]) for i in range(L)]
    while len(cs) % 7:
        cs.append("")
    o = [HDR]
    for j in range(0, len(cs), 7):
        o.append(" ".join(c.rjust(3) for c in cs[j:j + 7]).rstrip())
    return o


def bumped(m):
    """the scorer's rule: the middles of a run of >= 3 bump on to the next free day"""
    L = len(m)
    e = list(m)
    mv = []
    for i in range(1, L - 1):
        if "." not in (m[i - 1], m[i], m[i + 1]):
            j = i + 1
            while j < L and e[j] != ".":
                j += 1
            if j < L:
                e[i] = ">"
                e[j] = m[i]
            mv.append((i, j if j < L else -1))
    return e, mv


def runs_of(m):
    out = []
    i = 0
    while i < len(m):
        if m[i] != ".":
            j = i
            while j < len(m) and m[j] != ".":
                j += 1
            out.append((i, j - i))
            i = j
        else:
            i += 1
    return out


BIG = {0: [[]], 1: [[3]], 2: [[4]], 3: [[4, 3], [4, 3], [5]], 4: [[5, 3], [4, 4]]}


def generate(seed):
    r = random.Random(seed)
    n = 0 if r.random() < 0.12 else r.choice([1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4])
    for _ in range(400):
        L = r.choice([28, 29, 30, 31, 30, 31])
        S = r.randrange(7)
        blocks = r.choice(BIG[n]) + [2] * r.randint(2, 4) + [1] * r.randint(2, 4)
        if sum(l + max(1, l - 2) for l in blocks) + 2 > L:
            continue
        r.shuffle(blocks)
        pos = r.randrange(3)
        spots = []
        for l in blocks:
            if (pos + S) // 7 != (pos + l - 1 + S) // 7:
                pos = ((pos + S) // 7 + 1) * 7 - S      # a busy run never crosses a week row
            if pos + l - 1 >= L:
                spots = None
                break
            spots.append((pos, l))
            pos += l + max(1, l - 2) + (r.random() < 0.3) + (r.random() < 0.15)
        if spots is None:
            continue
        pool = r.sample(string.ascii_uppercase, 5)
        m = ["."] * L
        for a, l in spots:
            w = r.sample(pool, l) if l > 2 else [r.choice(pool) for _ in range(l)]
            for i in range(l):
                m[a + i] = w[i]
        e, mv = bumped(m)
        if len(mv) != n or any(j < 0 for _i, j in mv):
            continue
        if n > 1 and not any((S + j) % 7 > 4 for _i, j in mv):
            continue                                    # one bump always lands at a weekend
        R = runs_of(m)
        E = L - m.count(".")
        if not (8 <= E <= 17):
            continue
        if n and n in (E, len(R), L - E, len(set(m)) - 1, max(q[1] for q in R),
                       len([q for q in R if q[1] == 2]), len([q for q in R if q[1] == 1]),
                       len([q for q in R if q[1] >= 2]), len(page(m, S, L)) - 1,
                       len([i for i in range(L) if m[i] != "." and (S + i) % 7 > 4])):
            continue                                    # counts a player could read off instead
        return "\n".join(page(m, S, L) + ["%d bump" % n])
    return FB
solve:
HDR = " ".join(w.rjust(3) for w in "Mo Tu We Th Fr Sa Su".split())


def solve(clue):
    C = clue.split("\n")
    Q = [l.split() for l in C[1:-1]]
    m = [t[-1] for q in Q for t in q]
    L = len(m)
    S = 7 - len(Q[0])
    e = list(m)
    for i in range(1, L - 1):          # the middles of a run of >= 3 bump on
        if "." not in (m[i - 1], m[i], m[i + 1]):
            j = i + 1
            while j < L and e[j] != ".":
                j += 1
            if j < L:
                e[i] = ">"
                e[j] = m[i]
        # the day it leaves keeps a ">"; its letter is written again where it lands
    cs = [""] * S + ["%d%s" % (i + 1, e[i]) for i in range(L)]
    while len(cs) % 7:
        cs.append("")
    o = [HDR]
    for j in range(0, len(cs), 7):
        o.append(" ".join(c.rjust(3) for c in cs[j:j + 7]).rstrip())
    return "\n".join(o + [C[-1]])
